newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy in favour of "prudent dialogue" with Libya.
newsitem.headline: Italy in favour of "prudent dialogue" with Libya.

text.p: Italy wants to pursue a policy of "prudent dialogue" with Libya to encourage its leader Muammar Gaddafi to democratise and disavow terrorism, deputy foreign minister Piero Fassino said on Friday.
In remarks that threw up policy differences with the United States over how to deal with Gaddafi, Fassino said isolation was not the most effective instrument to bring about change.
"Today there are signs that the people in government in Tripoli are more disposed towards a (political) evolution than they were 10 years ago or five years ago," Fassino said.

"I believe it is wise and intelligent to seize all the room there is, the windows, opportunities to favour that evolution," he said in an interview with Nightly Business Report, a programme aired in the United States and produced in association with Reuters.
Fassino is one of three deputies at the foreign ministry and is responsible for European affairs.
His comments reinforced signals that the six-month-old centre-left government in Italy is cautiously working to try to ease the North African country out of its isolation.

Italy imports about one third of its oil from Libya and state energy giant ENI is the major foreign operator there, accounting for 17 percent of the production in 1995. ENI recently signed a $3 billion gas supply deal with Libya.
Fassino's interview coincided with heated speculation in Italy that Gaddafi may come to Rome next week to attend the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation World Food Summit.
Senior foreign ministry officials and FAO all say they have no indication about the make-up of the Libyan delegation but have not ruled out what would be a stunning visit by Gaddafi.

The United States has a long list of grievances against Libya, including its refusal to surrender two Libyans accused of blowing up Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland in 1988, 270 people aboard the plane and the ground.
Libya has since 1992 been under U.N. sanctions, including an air and arms embargo, over the Lockerbie case, and the U.S. imposed economic sanctions on it more than 10 years ago.

President Bill Clinton, elected this week to a second term, signed a law in August aimed at preventing new foreign investment in Libya and Iran, two countries which Washington believes back "international terrorism".
Fassino said all states had to have a "clear, precise line" against terrorism and should face sanctions where their attitude was ambiguous or one of complicity.
But he added: "Naturally, precisely because you have to be so determined, every time you accuse a country of terrorism you have to be in a position to demonstrate it and prove it."

"You have to evaluate case by case, and moment by moment, how to graduate ties with countries that are ambiguous on this issue in relation to the evolution of their political situation and also to the ability to influence their political situation."
Fassino said that U.S. relations with Syria, which Washington has in the past accused of sponsoring terrorism, were different now from 10 years ago.
"So Italy thinks that you have to a policy of prudent dialogue towards Libya aimed at favouring the country's political evolution," he added.

Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said last month that Italy would support a review of a European Union decision to exclude Libya from a cooperation agreement between the EU and countries of the Mediterranean once the time was right.

His olive branch followed a visit to Cairo by Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who said Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak had tried to persuade him that Gaddafi had changed his attitude to the West and was now trying to be cooperative.
"President Mubarak insisted on the limits of the politics of embargo, especially with Libya," Prodi said then.
